blocks.title: Why Function Calling and Tool Use matters here

spans.text: Problem statement: A customer agent needs to look up orders, issue refunds, and stop before risky actions. The learner's job is not to memorize Function Calling and Tool Use; it is to decide what to build or change, what evidence the system may use, and how to tell whether the change improved valid tool calls with safe stop behavior.

Running case: function-calling contract with tool schemas and confirmation rules. We will keep this same case through the lesson so each idea has a job: frame the problem, explain the mechanism, choose a design, test the implementation, and decide what to do next.

Before reading on, predict: if the model calls refund_user without required approval data, where would you look first - the input, the state or data, the model boundary, the validation check, or the release process?
The lesson assumes you can learn the vocabulary, then spends its effort on integration choices, failure signals, and checks that make the idea usable in a real system.

items.text: Product framing: Function Calling and Tool Use matters when it changes a user-visible decision, release gate, or operational workflow.
Engineering framing: Function Calling and Tool Use matters when it changes data, state, prompts, model behavior, tools, schemas, traces, or runtime constraints.
Validation framing: the lesson is not complete until the team can measure valid tool calls with safe stop behavior on examples that resemble the real workload.

blocks.title: Fully worked example: function-calling contract with tool schemas and confirmation rules

spans.text: Scenario: A customer agent needs to look up orders, issue refunds, and stop before risky actions. The team wants to improve valid tool calls with safe stop behavior, but it has already seen this failure: the model calls refund_user without required approval data.
Here is the worked artifact at design-review depth: concrete enough to inspect, small enough to build as a thin slice.
Complete worked artifact

items.text: Debug case: a long customer request includes the JSON rules near the beginning, then thousands of tokens of detail. The model returns prose instead of valid JSON because the relevant instruction is weak, crowded, or outside useful context.

Artifact: function-calling contract with tool schemas and confirmation rules. It contains the prompt layout, important tokens, context-window risk, output schema, validator, and a repair or escalation rule for valid tool calls with safe stop behavior.
Worked output: put the schema next to the final instruction, keep examples short, validate the returned JSON, and fail closed when required fields are missing.

spans.text: Complete AI-assistant prompt for this artifact

Role: LLM debugger. Context: A customer agent needs to look up orders, issue refunds, and stop before risky actions. Task: diagnose why the output violated the contract. Inspect prompt placement, context length, examples, schema, validator, and repair path. Output: {root_cause, prompt_change, validation_rule, test_cases, release_decision}.
Why this is richer than a definition
The example ties Function Calling and Tool Use to a specific input, output, decision, failure mode, and metric. That is the move you should repeat when applying the lesson to your own system.

blocks.title: Mechanism: the mechanism in the running case

spans.text: Mechanism opens the machinery behind Function Calling and Tool Use. In the running case, the important question is: what exactly changes between the user's request and the final output?
Mechanism means following tokens through the context window into next-token prediction, then checking whether the output contract survived.
Two framings for the same idea

items.text: Plain framing: imagine a reviewer following a checklist. They need to see what came in, what was considered, what was rejected, and why the final answer is safe to use.
Technical framing: imagine a trace. It should expose inputs, state, external evidence, model or algorithm output, validation result, and owner for exceptions.

blocks.title: Case study: what changed after the first review

spans.text: The first prototype works on the demo path. Then a reviewer runs the uncomfortable case: the model calls refund_user without required approval data. The output still looks confident, which is exactly why the lesson needs a richer artifact.

The team does not restart from scratch. It adds one missing control to function-calling contract with tool schemas and confirmation rules: a stricter input contract, better source metadata, a validation assertion, a human-review edge, a rollback trigger, or an audit log depending on where the failure appeared.

items.text: Decision made: keep the thin slice, but block release until the failure is observable and repeatable.
Evidence added: the artifact now shows the input, intermediate evidence, final output, and pass/fail reason.
Metric promoted: valid tool calls with safe stop behavior becomes part of the release gate instead of a dashboard someone checks later.

spans.text: Case-study takeaway: a useful Function Calling and Tool Use design makes the wrong answer inspectable before it reaches users.

spans.text: This is where Function Calling and Tool Use becomes a decision. The team must choose how much rigor function-calling contract with tool schemas and confirmation rules needs before it can be trusted.

The wrong move is to jump straight to the fanciest option. The useful move is to ask which option improves valid tool calls with safe stop behavior while making this failure visible: the model calls refund_user without required approval data.

blocks.title: How this breaks in practice

spans.text: The failure mode to keep in view is concrete: the model calls refund_user without required approval data. Use it as a diagnostic lens while reading every design choice.

items.text: The prompt is correct in isolation but buried outside the useful context of a long request.
The model returns JSON-shaped text that violates required fields or allowed values.
A repair loop hides the underlying prompt/schema problem instead of surfacing it.
The broad warning sign: valid tool calls with safe stop behavior gets worse even though the final answer or artifact still looks polished.

spans.text: Debugging rule: inspect the earliest place where bad evidence can enter and the latest place where validation should have stopped it.

blocks.useWhen: Use the production path when valid tool calls with safe stop behavior affects users, trust, safety, cost, or compliance.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid advanced optimization while the team still cannot reproduce or detect: the model calls refund_user without required approval data.
blocks.ruleOfThumb: Make the failure visible before making the system more sophisticated.

blocks.title: Tiny implementation sketch: make the contract concrete

spans.text: A useful implementation sketch for Function Calling and Tool Use should be small enough to inspect and real enough to fail. That means it needs a realistic input, an explicit decision boundary, and a visible output.

For function-calling contract with tool schemas and confirmation rules, the sketch should prove one thing: the system can improve valid tool calls with safe stop behavior without hiding the failure where the model calls refund_user without required approval data.
Predict before the code: should the system answer, retrieve more evidence, block, escalate, or mark the case inconclusive when this failure appears?

blocks.title: Runnable check: validate structured output
blocks.code:
# Function Calling and Tool Use: structured output validator.
import json
raw = '{"decision": "escalate", "confidence": 0.82, "reason": "missing invoice id"}'
required = {"decision", "confidence", "reason"}
allowed = {"answer", "escalate", "refuse"}
obj = json.loads(raw)
valid = required.issubset(obj) and obj["decision"] in allowed and 0 <= obj["confidence"] <= 1
print(obj["decision"])
print("valid" if valid else "invalid")

spans.text: This is a runnable miniature, not the whole production system. It makes the lesson's contract visible: input, decision rule, output, and a check related to the model calls refund_user without required approval data.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict the decision and validation result.
predictThenReveal.answer:
It prints:
escalate
valid

The output is not trusted because it looks like JSON. The validator checks fields, allowed values, and ranges before downstream code uses it.

blocks.title: Verify AI-generated work before trusting it

spans.text: If an AI assistant drafts code, a prompt, a workflow, or a policy for Function Calling and Tool Use, review it against the running case before accepting it.

items.text: Does it name the real artifact: function-calling contract with tool schemas and confirmation rules?
Does it include a realistic input and a concrete expected output?
Does it test or block the known failure: the model calls refund_user without required approval data?
Does it expose enough evidence to debug valid tool calls with safe stop behavior?
Does it define what happens when evidence is missing: retry, refuse, ask a human, roll back, or mark the case inconclusive?
